options.text: relax the detrusor and contract the internal sphincter

options.label: C
options.text: contract both detrusor and internal sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: have no effect on the detrusor

options.label: E
options.text: act only on the external sphincter

questions.why: Pelvic splanchnic (S2-S4) parasympathetic activity empties the bladder: detrusor contraction with internal-sphincter relaxation.

questions.stem: Sympathetic fibres via the hypogastric plexus promote bladder filling by

options.label: B
options.text: relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter

options.label: E
options.text: contracting the detrusor and relaxing the internal sphincter

questions.why: Sympathetic activity relaxes the detrusor and contracts the internal urethral sphincter, favouring storage.

questions.stem: The internal urethral sphincter in the male serves the additional function of
questions.why: The male internal sphincter (smooth muscle, sympathetic T11-L2) also prevents retrograde ejaculation.

questions.stem: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle supplied by the
questions.why: The voluntary external sphincter in the urogenital diaphragm is innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4).

questions.stem: The female urethra is short (3-4 cm), which clinically means
questions.why: The short female urethra predisposes to ascending UTI and is easy to catheterize.

questions.stem: The female urethra opens into the vestibule
questions.why: The external urethral orifice lies in the vestibule, anterior to the vaginal opening and behind the clitoris.

questions.stem: The paraurethral (Skene's) glands of the female urethra are the developmental homologue of the
questions.why: Skene's (paraurethral) glands are the female homologue of the prostate.

questions.stem: The longest and widest, most dilatable part of the male urethra is the
questions.why: The prostatic urethra (~3 cm) is the widest and most dilatable part, receiving the prostatic and ejaculatory ducts.

questions.stem: The narrowest and least dilatable part of the male urethra, most liable to rupture during catheterization, is the
questions.why: The membranous urethra (~2 cm), passing through the urogenital diaphragm, is the narrowest and least dilatable.

questions.stem: The spongy (penile) urethra receives the ducts of which glands?
questions.why: The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands open into the spongy urethra; the ejaculatory and prostatic ducts open into the prostatic urethra.

questions.stem: The prostatic utricle, opening on the seminal colliculus, is a remnant of the
questions.why: The prostatic utricle is the male remnant of the fused paramesonephric ducts (homologue of uterus/vagina).

questions.stem: The spongy urethra drains lymph mainly to the
questions.why: The spongy (penile) urethra drains to the inguinal nodes; the prostatic and membranous parts drain to internal iliac nodes.

questions.stem: Physiological urinary incontinence in infants occurs because
questions.why: Voluntary sphincter control awaits myelination of the corticospinal tracts, developing by about 3-6 years.

questions.stem: Most urinary tract stones (about 75%) are composed of
questions.why: About 75% of stones are calcium oxalate/phosphate; struvite (~15%) and uric acid/cystine (~10%) are less common.

questions.stem: Disintegration of a urinary stone using focused external shock waves is called
questions.why: Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy fragments stones without open surgery.

questions.stem: A transplanted kidney is usually placed in the
questions.why: Renal transplants are placed in the iliac fossa, with anastomosis to the iliac vessels and bladder.

questions.stem: A congenital fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys, trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery, is a
questions.why: A horseshoe kidney is caught beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent and remains low.

questions.stem: The olfactory nerve fibres (CN I) reach the olfactory bulb by passing through the
questions.why: CN I fibres pass through the perforations of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

questions.stem: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve together with the
questions.why: The optic canal carries CN II and the ophthalmic artery.

questions.stem: Which set of nerves all pass through the superior orbital fissure?
questions.why: The oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic (V1) and abducens nerves (plus the superior ophthalmic vein) traverse the superior orbital fissure.

questions.stem: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) leaves the middle cranial fossa through the
questions.why: V2 exits via the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa; V3 exits via the foramen ovale.

questions.stem: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through the
questions.why: The middle meningeal artery (and meningeal branch of V3) passes through the foramen spinosum.

questions.stem: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves leave the skull together through the
questions.why: CN IX, X and XI exit via the jugular foramen with the internal jugular vein.

questions.stem: The facial nerve emerges onto the face region through the
questions.why: CN VII exits the skull base through the stylomastoid foramen (after giving chorda tympani within the temporal bone).

questions.stem: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exits the skull through the
questions.why: CN XII leaves through the hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone.

questions.stem: The internal carotid artery enters the skull base through the
questions.why: The ICA enters through the carotid canal (and crosses the upper part of the foramen lacerum, which nothing fully traverses).

questions.stem: The spinal roots of the accessory nerve (CN XI) enter the cranial cavity through the
questions.why: The spinal roots of CN XI ascend through the foramen magnum, then leave with IX and X via the jugular foramen.

questions.stem: The pterion is clinically important because deep to it runs the
questions.why: A blow fracturing the thin pterion may tear the underlying anterior division of the middle meningeal artery, giving an extradural haematoma.

questions.stem: The point where the coronal and sagittal sutures meet is the
questions.why: Bregma is the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures; lambda is where the sagittal meets the lambdoid.

questions.stem: Emissary veins passing through the skull are clinically significant because they

options.label: A
options.text: carry cerebrospinal fluid to the scalp

options.label: C
options.text: link scalp veins to the dural venous sinuses

options.label: D
options.text: supply the diploe with arterial blood

options.label: E
options.text: drain the brain to the facial vein alone

questions.why: Valveless emissary veins link extracranial (scalp) veins with the dural venous sinuses, a route for spread of infection.

questions.stem: The five layers of the scalp, from superficial to deep, are Skin, dense Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue and
questions.why: The scalp layers spell SCALP: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis (galea), Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.

questions.stem: Scalp wounds bleed profusely because the vessels lie in the dense connective tissue layer, where they are

options.label: E
options.text: held open by fibrous septa and cannot retract

questions.why: Fibrous septa of the second (dense connective tissue) layer anchor the vessel walls open, preventing retraction and vasospasm.

questions.stem: The 'dangerous area' of the scalp, through which infection may spread to the cranial venous sinuses, is the
questions.why: The loose areolar layer transmits emissary veins to the intracranial sinuses, so infection here can spread inward.

questions.stem: A deep scalp laceration gapes widely only when the wound cuts transversely through the
questions.why: Transverse cuts through the galea aponeurotica let the occipitofrontalis pull the edges apart; cuts sparing it do not gape.

questions.stem: The muscles of facial expression develop from the second pharyngeal arch and are therefore supplied by the
questions.why: Facial expression muscles are second-arch derivatives supplied by CN VII; the muscles of mastication (first arch) are supplied by V3.

questions.stem: The 'danger area of the face' can spread infection to the cavernous sinus because the facial vein communicates with it via the
questions.why: The valveless facial vein links to the cavernous sinus through the superior ophthalmic vein, so infection in the nasolabial region can spread intracranially.

questions.stem: Within the parotid gland, the most superficial of the three major structures is the
questions.why: From superficial to deep the parotid contains the facial nerve, then the retromandibular vein, then the external carotid artery.

questions.stem: The chief muscle of the cheek, which keeps food on the occlusal surfaces during chewing, is the
questions.why: The buccinator (CN VII) compresses the cheek against the teeth; although it aids chewing it is a muscle of facial expression.

questions.stem: The superficial temporal artery is one of the two terminal branches of the
questions.why: The external carotid artery ends as the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries.

questions.stem: Giant cell (temporal) arteritis most characteristically involves the
questions.why: Temporal arteritis typically affects the superficial temporal artery, giving a tender, thickened, pulseless vessel.

questions.stem: The maxillary artery enters the infratemporal fossa by passing deep to the neck of the mandible, between it and the
questions.why: The maxillary artery passes between the neck of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament.

questions.stem: The branch of the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery that runs to the mandibular foramen is the
questions.why: The inferior alveolar artery (first part) enters the mandibular foramen; the middle meningeal (also first part) goes to the foramen spinosum.

questions.stem: The valveless pterygoid venous plexus is clinically important because it communicates with the cavernous sinus through the
questions.why: Emissary veins through the foramina ovale and Vesalius link the pterygoid plexus to the cavernous sinus, a route for infection.

questions.stem: The auriculotemporal nerve conveys postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland from the
questions.why: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the otic ganglion hitch-hike on the auriculotemporal nerve (V3) to the parotid.

questions.stem: The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa to carry taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibres to the
questions.why: Chorda tympani (from CN VII) carries taste and preganglionic parasympathetic fibres (relaying in the submandibular ganglion) to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

questions.stem: The nerve to the medial pterygoid also supplies motor fibres to the tensor tympani and the
questions.why: The nerve to medial pterygoid (from the main trunk of V3) also supplies tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

questions.stem: Which muscle of mastication is the only one that protrudes the mandible and initiates jaw opening?
questions.why: The lateral pterygoid protrudes the mandible and begins depression (opening); the others close the jaw.

questions.stem: The retromandibular vein is formed within the parotid region by union of the superficial temporal vein and the
questions.why: The superficial temporal and maxillary veins unite to form the retromandibular vein.

questions.stem: The pterygopalatine fossa is a pyramidal space lying behind the maxilla and below the

options.label: C
options.text: floor of the middle cranial fossa

questions.why: The pterygopalatine fossa lies behind the maxilla, below the orbital apex, acting as a neurovascular crossroads.

questions.stem: The anterior wall of the pterygopalatine fossa is formed by the

options.label: A
options.text: pyramidal process of the palatine bone

options.label: E
options.text: perpendicular plate of the palatine bone

questions.why: The posterior surface of the maxilla forms the anterior wall; the pterygoid process forms the posterior wall.

questions.stem: Which opening in the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa leads directly into the nasal cavity?
questions.why: The sphenopalatine foramen (medial wall) opens into the nasal cavity; foramen rotundum opens to the middle cranial fossa.

questions.stem: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the orbit through the
questions.why: The inferior orbital fissure connects the pterygopalatine fossa to the floor of the orbit.

questions.stem: The main parasympathetic (motor) root of the pterygopalatine ganglion is the
questions.why: The greater petrosal nerve (from CN VII) carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibres that synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.stem: The nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve) is formed by union of the greater petrosal nerve and the
questions.why: The Vidian nerve = greater petrosal (parasympathetic) + deep petrosal (sympathetic).

questions.stem: The deep petrosal nerve carries which type of fibres into the pterygoid canal?
questions.why: The deep petrosal nerve carries postganglionic sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus, which pass through the ganglion without synapsing.

questions.stem: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion supply the lacrimal, nasal and palatine glands but NOT the
questions.why: The submandibular (and sublingual) glands are supplied by the submandibular ganglion, not the pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.stem: The nerve usually regarded as the direct continuation of the maxillary nerve beyond the pterygopalatine fossa is the
questions.why: V2 continues as the infraorbital nerve through the inferior orbital fissure and infraorbital canal.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic fibres reach the lacrimal gland from the pterygopalatine ganglion by travelling on the zygomatic nerve and then a communicating branch to the
questions.why: Secretomotor fibres hop from the zygomatic branch of V2 to the lacrimal nerve (V1) to reach the lacrimal gland.

questions.stem: A maxillary nerve block placed in the pterygopalatine fossa would numb the

options.label: B
options.text: lower eyelid, upper lip and nasal cavity

options.label: C
options.text: chin, lower lip and anterior tongue

questions.why: V2 supplies the mid-face: lower eyelid, upper lip, upper teeth, palate and nasal cavity.

questions.stem: The greater palatine nerve, a branch of the pterygopalatine ganglion, supplies the

options.label: E
options.text: anterior palatal gingiva to the canines

questions.why: The greater palatine nerve supplies most of the hard-palate mucosa and gingiva; the nasopalatine supplies the anterior palate behind the incisors.

questions.stem: The atlas (C1) is unusual among vertebrae in that it has no
questions.why: C1 has no body and no true spinous process; it is a ring of two lateral masses joined by anterior and posterior arches.

questions.stem: The dens (odontoid process) is a distinguishing feature of the
questions.why: The dens projects upward from the body of the axis (C2) and forms the pivot for the atlanto-axial joint.

questions.stem: A long, non-bifid spinous process that is easily palpated at the base of the neck identifies the
questions.why: C7, the vertebra prominens, has a long non-bifid spinous process used as a surface landmark.

questions.stem: A feature unique to cervical vertebrae, transmitting the vertebral artery, is the
questions.why: Each cervical transverse process contains a foramen transversarium; those of C1-C6 transmit the vertebral artery.

questions.stem: Nodding the head ('yes' movement) occurs chiefly at the
questions.why: Flexion-extension (nodding) occurs at the condyloid atlanto-occipital joints; rotation ('no') occurs at the atlanto-axial joint.

questions.stem: The ligament that holds the dens tightly against the anterior arch of the atlas is the
questions.why: The transverse ligament of the atlas retains the dens; the alar ligaments limit rotation and the apical ligament is a small median band.

questions.stem: A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the anterior and posterior arches of which vertebra?
questions.why: A vertical blow to the vertex produces the Jefferson (burst) fracture of the C1 ring; the cord is often spared because the canal is wide.

questions.stem: A hangman's fracture passes bilaterally through the pars interarticularis of the
questions.why: Forceful hyperextension with distraction fractures the pars interarticularis of C2 (hangman's fracture).

questions.stem: The hyoid bone is unique among the bones of the body because it
questions.why: The U-shaped hyoid has no bony articulations; it is suspended by muscles and ligaments at the level of C3.

questions.stem: Fracture of the hyoid bone is a classic forensic indicator of
questions.why: Because the hyoid is well protected, its fracture strongly suggests manual (hands-on) strangulation.

questions.stem: The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius both receive their motor supply from the
questions.why: CN XI gives motor supply to SCM and trapezius; the cervical plexus provides only sensory (proprioceptive) fibres.

questions.stem: The platysma, a muscle of the superficial neck, is supplied by the
questions.why: Platysma is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the cervical branch of CN VII.

questions.stem: Most of the infrahyoid ('strap') muscles are innervated by the
questions.why: Sternohyoid, sternothyroid and omohyoid are supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3); thyrohyoid gets C1 fibres via CN XII.

questions.stem: The only infrahyoid muscle NOT supplied by the ansa cervicalis is the thyrohyoid, which is supplied by
questions.why: Thyrohyoid (and geniohyoid) receive C1 fibres travelling with CN XII.

questions.stem: The mylohyoid muscle, which forms the floor of the mouth, is supplied by the
questions.why: The nerve to mylohyoid, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), supplies mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric.

questions.stem: The posterior belly of the digastric muscle is supplied by the
questions.why: The anterior belly is supplied by V3 (nerve to mylohyoid) and the posterior belly by CN VII, reflecting their arch origins.

questions.stem: All four suboccipital muscles are supplied by the
questions.why: The suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1) is motor to all four suboccipital muscles.

questions.stem: The anterior scalene is an important landmark because the phrenic nerve
questions.why: The phrenic nerve passes vertically downward on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene.

questions.stem: The roots and trunks of the brachial plexus, with the subclavian artery, emerge between the anterior scalene and the
questions.why: The interscalene triangle between anterior and middle scalene transmits the brachial plexus and subclavian artery.

questions.stem: The posterior triangle of the neck is bounded anteriorly by the SCM and posteriorly by the

options.label: D
options.text: anterior border of trapezius and the clavicle

questions.why: Posterior triangle: anterior = posterior border of SCM, posterior = anterior border of trapezius, base = middle third of clavicle.

questions.stem: A nerve especially vulnerable during a lymph-node biopsy in the posterior triangle is the
questions.why: CN XI runs superficially across the posterior triangle and may be injured in node biopsy, causing trapezius weakness.

questions.stem: The carotid triangle is so named because it contains the

options.label: B
options.text: bifurcation of the common carotid artery

questions.why: The carotid triangle contains the carotid bifurcation and the beginning of the internal and external carotid arteries.

questions.stem: The submental triangle is unpaired because it is bounded by the body of the hyoid and the
questions.why: The submental triangle lies between the two anterior bellies of digastric and the hyoid, crossing the midline.

questions.stem: The anterior triangle of the neck is subdivided by the digastric and the superior belly of omohyoid into the carotid, muscular, submental and
questions.why: The four subdivisions of the anterior triangle are the carotid, muscular, submental and submandibular (digastric) triangles.

questions.stem: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the
questions.why: The cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; the RLN supplies all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

questions.stem: The four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge at the midpoint of the posterior border of the SCM, a site called
questions.why: Erb's point (nerve point of the neck) is where the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge; used for a cervical plexus block.

questions.stem: The phrenic nerve, the sole motor supply to the diaphragm, arises mainly from spinal segment
questions.why: The phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5, mainly C4 ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive').

questions.stem: The ansa cervicalis is formed by fibres from spinal nerves
questions.why: The ansa cervicalis (superior and inferior roots) is formed by C1-C3 and supplies the infrahyoid muscles.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve descends within the carotid sheath throughout the neck?
questions.why: CN X runs the length of the carotid sheath between and behind the carotid artery and internal jugular vein.

questions.stem: The great auricular nerve, a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus, supplies skin over the
questions.why: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) supplies skin over the parotid, the angle of the jaw and the lower auricle.

questions.stem: The common carotid artery usually bifurcates at the level of the
questions.why: The CCA divides into internal and external carotid arteries at about C4, the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.

questions.stem: Which artery gives no branches in the neck?
questions.why: The internal carotid artery ascends to the skull without branching in the neck; the external carotid gives several branches.

questions.stem: The vertebral artery most commonly arises from the
questions.why: The vertebral artery is the first branch of the first part of the subclavian artery and ascends through the foramina transversaria.

questions.stem: The inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the
questions.why: The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.

questions.stem: Carotid sinus massage slows the heart because it stimulates baroreceptors supplied by the
questions.why: Baroreceptors of the carotid sinus are supplied by CN IX; their stimulation raises vagal tone and slows the heart.

questions.stem: The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as a continuation of the
questions.why: The IJV begins as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus at the jugular foramen.

questions.stem: The external jugular vein is formed by the posterior auricular vein and the

options.label: B
options.text: posterior division of the retromandibular vein

options.label: C
options.text: anterior division of the retromandibular vein

questions.why: The EJV = posterior auricular vein + posterior division of the retromandibular vein; it crosses the SCM superficially.

questions.stem: The right internal jugular vein is preferred for central venous catheterisation mainly because it has

options.label: B
options.text: no relation to the carotid artery

options.label: C
options.text: a straighter path to the SVC

options.label: D
options.text: a wider lumen than the left

questions.why: The right IJV gives a nearly straight line to the SVC and avoids the thoracic duct, which drains at the left venous angle.

questions.stem: The jugulodigastric (tonsillar) node is typically the first to enlarge in
questions.why: The jugulodigastric node drains the tonsil and pharynx and enlarges early in tonsillitis and oropharyngeal cancer.

questions.stem: An enlarged, firm, non-tender left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node suggests metastatic cancer of the
questions.why: Virchow's node receives lymph via the thoracic duct from the abdomen; Troisier's sign points to gastric and other abdominal malignancy.

questions.stem: The jugulo-omohyoid node is particularly associated with lymph drainage from the
questions.why: The jugulo-omohyoid node is the 'lymph node of the tongue', often the first involved in tongue carcinoma.

questions.stem: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia splits to enclose the trapezius and the
questions.why: The investing layer surrounds the neck like a collar, splitting to ensheath the SCM and trapezius and the parotid and submandibular glands.

questions.stem: The pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia encloses the

options.label: B
options.text: internal jugular vein and phrenic nerve

questions.why: The visceral pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid, larynx, trachea, pharynx and cervical oesophagus.

questions.stem: The carotid sheath encloses the common/internal carotid artery, the vagus nerve and the
questions.why: The carotid sheath contains the carotid artery, IJV and CN X; the sympathetic trunk lies behind it, not within it.

questions.stem: Infection in the 'danger space' is clinically feared because it can spread directly to the
questions.why: The danger space (between alar and prevertebral fasciae) runs from the skull base to the diaphragm, allowing spread to the posterior mediastinum.

questions.stem: The cervical sympathetic trunk lies on the surface of which fascia?
questions.why: The sympathetic trunk lies on the prevertebral fascia, behind (deep to) the carotid sheath.

questions.stem: The thyroid isthmus typically crosses in front of which tracheal rings?
questions.why: The isthmus usually overlies the 2nd-4th tracheal rings, a landmark for tracheostomy.

questions.stem: A pyramidal lobe of the thyroid, when present, is a remnant of the
questions.why: The pyramidal lobe represents a persistent lower part of the thyroglossal duct.

questions.stem: Calcitonin is secreted by the
questions.why: Parafollicular (C) cells secrete calcitonin; follicular cells make T3 and T4.

questions.stem: The nerve most at risk of injury during thyroidectomy, running near the groove between trachea and oesophagus, is the
questions.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerve lies in or near the tracheo-oesophageal groove and may be injured in thyroid surgery.

questions.stem: The superior parathyroid glands develop embryologically from the
questions.why: Superior parathyroids arise from the 4th pouches; the inferior parathyroids (and thymus) arise from the 3rd pouches.

questions.stem: The inferior parathyroid glands are more variable in position and may descend into the
questions.why: Because of their longer embryological descent with the thymus, inferior parathyroids may be found in the superior mediastinum.

questions.stem: A Pancoast tumour at the lung apex may cause Horner's syndrome by compressing the
questions.why: An apical lung tumour can compress the stellate ganglion, interrupting sympathetic supply to the head and neck.

questions.stem: Postganglionic sympathetic fibres to the dilator pupillae and other orbital structures travel from the superior cervical ganglion along the
questions.why: Fibres run with the internal carotid artery as the internal carotid (carotid) plexus to reach the orbit.

questions.stem: In the cervical sympathetic trunk, the preganglionic fibres that synapse in the superior cervical ganglion originate from the
questions.why: No white rami enter the cervical ganglia; preganglionic fibres ascend from upper thoracic (T1-T6) segments to synapse there.

questions.stem: The fragile 'lamina papyracea' that forms most of the medial wall of the orbit is part of the
questions.why: The lamina papyracea is the paper-thin orbital plate of the ethmoid, lying next to the ethmoidal air cells.

questions.stem: The roof of the orbit is formed mainly by the orbital plate of the frontal bone and the
questions.why: The roof is formed by the frontal bone's orbital plate and the lesser wing of the sphenoid.

questions.stem: The common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn) is the common origin of the
questions.why: The four recti arise from the annulus of Zinn, which surrounds the optic canal at the orbital apex.

questions.stem: Which structure passes through the superior orbital fissure OUTSIDE the common tendinous ring?
questions.why: CN IV, the frontal and lacrimal nerves and the superior ophthalmic vein pass outside the ring; III, VI and nasociliary pass through it.

questions.stem: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve and the
questions.why: The optic canal, in the lesser wing of the sphenoid, carries CN II and the ophthalmic artery.

questions.stem: The lateral rectus muscle is supplied by the
questions.why: Remember LR6 SO4, the rest 3: lateral rectus = CN VI, superior oblique = CN IV, all others = CN III.

questions.stem: The superior oblique muscle is supplied by the
questions.why: The superior oblique is the only extraocular muscle supplied by CN IV (the trochlear nerve).

questions.stem: The tendon of the superior oblique muscle changes direction by passing through a fibrocartilaginous pulley called the
questions.why: The superior oblique tendon loops through the trochlea on the medial orbital roof before inserting on the sclera.

questions.stem: To test the superior rectus in isolation, the patient is asked to look
questions.why: Clinically the superior rectus is tested with the eye abducted (looking up and laterally), isolating its elevating action.

questions.stem: The muscle that elevates the upper eyelid under voluntary (somatic) control is the
questions.why: Levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) is the main voluntary elevator; the superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle is a smooth, sympathetically-driven accessory.

questions.stem: Drooping of the eyelid (ptosis) in Horner's syndrome results from loss of sympathetic supply to the
questions.why: The partial ptosis of Horner's syndrome is due to paralysis of the sympathetically-innervated superior tarsal muscle.

questions.stem: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres for pupillary constriction arise from the
questions.why: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus sends preganglionic fibres via CN III to the ciliary ganglion.

questions.stem: Postganglionic parasympathetic fibres reach the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle via the
questions.why: From the ciliary ganglion, postganglionic parasympathetic fibres travel in the short ciliary nerves to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.

questions.stem: Dilation of the pupil (mydriasis) is produced by the dilator pupillae under
questions.why: The radial dilator pupillae is sympathetically driven; the circular sphincter pupillae is parasympathetic.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic secretomotor supply to the lacrimal gland originates in the
questions.why: Lacrimal secretomotor fibres leave CN VII via the greater petrosal nerve, synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion, then hitch-hike on V2 and V1 to the gland.

questions.stem: Tears drain from the lacrimal sac into the nasal cavity through the nasolacrimal duct, which opens into the
questions.why: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus beneath the inferior concha.

questions.stem: The correct order of tear drainage from the eye surface is

options.label: B
options.text: puncta, canaliculi, lacrimal sac, nasolacrimal duct

questions.why: Tears flow: lacrimal puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus.

questions.stem: The lacrimal gland lies in the
questions.why: The lacrimal gland occupies the superolateral orbit, in the lacrimal fossa of the frontal bone.

questions.stem: Aqueous humour is produced by the

options.label: A
options.text: the choroid plexus of the eye

questions.why: The ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour into the posterior chamber; it then flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber.

questions.stem: Aqueous humour drains from the anterior chamber through the trabecular meshwork into the
questions.why: At the iridocorneal angle, aqueous humour passes through the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm.

questions.stem: The outer fibrous tunic of the eyeball consists of the sclera and the
questions.why: The fibrous layer is the sclera (posterior 5/6) plus the transparent cornea (anterior 1/6).

questions.stem: The vascular (uveal) layer of the eyeball is composed of the choroid, ciliary body and
questions.why: The uvea comprises the choroid, ciliary body and iris.

questions.stem: The cornea is well suited to transplantation chiefly because it is
questions.why: Being avascular, the cornea has limited immune access, giving corneal grafts a high success rate.

questions.stem: The region of sharpest visual acuity, containing only cones, is the
questions.why: The fovea centralis, a pit within the macula, contains only cones and gives the sharpest acuity.

questions.stem: The optic disc is the 'blind spot' because it
questions.why: The optic disc is where the optic nerve leaves and vessels enter; it has no photoreceptors.

questions.stem: Rod photoreceptors contain the photopigment
questions.why: Rods contain rhodopsin and mediate scotopic (low-light) vision; cones contain photopsins for colour vision.

questions.stem: Accommodation for near vision is produced by contraction of the
questions.why: Parasympathetic contraction of the ciliary muscle slackens the zonular fibres, letting the lens become more convex for near focus.

questions.stem: Clouding (opacification) of the lens is called a
questions.why: A cataract is opacification of the lens; glaucoma is raised intraocular pressure.

questions.stem: The meibomian (tarsal) glands are embedded within the
questions.why: Modified sebaceous meibomian glands lie within the tarsal plates and secrete the lipid layer of the tear film.

questions.stem: A painless firm nodule in the eyelid caused by chronic blockage of a meibomian gland is a
questions.why: A chalazion is a painless granuloma of a blocked meibomian gland, away from the lid margin; a stye (hordeolum) is acute and painful at the margin.

questions.stem: The thin fascial sheath that surrounds the eyeball and separates it from orbital fat is
questions.why: Tenon's capsule (fascia bulbi) envelops the globe from the optic nerve to the corneoscleral junction.

questions.stem: The skin of the lower eyelid is supplied mainly by the
questions.why: The infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the lower-lid skin; the upper lid is supplied by branches of V1.

questions.stem: The lobule (earlobe) of the auricle differs from the rest of the pinna in that it
questions.why: The pinna is elastic cartilage except the lobule, which contains only fibrofatty tissue and skin.

questions.stem: During otoscopy in an adult the auricle is pulled
questions.why: Pulling the adult auricle up and back straightens the cartilaginous external acoustic meatus for examination.

questions.stem: The outer third of the external acoustic meatus is cartilaginous, while the inner two-thirds is
questions.why: The lateral third is cartilaginous; the medial two-thirds is bone (temporal bone).

questions.stem: The part of the tympanic membrane that lacks the fibrous middle layer is the
questions.why: The pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane) lacks the fibrous layer and is more flexible; the pars tensa is the main vibrating part.

questions.stem: On otoscopy the 'cone of light' is a reflection seen in the
questions.why: The light reflex radiates anteroinferiorly from the umbo on the normal tympanic membrane.

questions.stem: The medial (labyrinthine) wall of the middle ear bears a rounded prominence, the promontory, formed by the
questions.why: The promontory on the medial wall is produced by the basal turn of the cochlea and carries the tympanic plexus.

questions.stem: The roof (tegmental wall) of the middle ear, separating it from the middle cranial fossa, is the
questions.why: The tegmen tympani of the petrous temporal bone forms the roof of the tympanic cavity.

questions.stem: The base (footplate) of the stapes is attached to the oval window by the
questions.why: The stapes footplate is fixed in the oval window by the annular ligament (a syndesmosis).

questions.stem: Which muscle, supplied by the facial nerve, dampens movement of the stapes at the oval window?
questions.why: Stapedius (CN VII), the smallest skeletal muscle, dampens the stapes; tensor tympani (V3) tenses the eardrum.

questions.stem: The tensor tympani muscle is supplied by the
questions.why: Tensor tympani is supplied by V3 (via the nerve to medial pterygoid); stapedius is supplied by CN VII.

questions.stem: Otitis media is more common in children because the pharyngotympanic (Eustachian) tube is
questions.why: A child's auditory tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal, easing spread of infection from the nasopharynx.

questions.stem: The auditory tube is actively opened during swallowing mainly by the
questions.why: Tensor veli palatini opens the tube; levator veli palatini and salpingopharyngeus assist.

questions.stem: The tympanic plexus on the promontory is formed mainly by the tympanic branch of the
questions.why: Jacobson's nerve (tympanic branch of CN IX) with sympathetic fibres forms the tympanic plexus; it continues as the lesser petrosal nerve.

questions.stem: The chorda tympani crosses the tympanic cavity between the
questions.why: The chorda tympani (CN VII) runs across the medial surface of the tympanic membrane between the handle of the malleus and the long process of the incus.

questions.stem: MacEwen's (suprameatal) triangle is a surgical landmark overlying the
questions.why: MacEwen's triangle is used in mastoidectomy as a safe entry to the mastoid antrum.

questions.stem: The bony labyrinth contains which fluid?
questions.why: Perilymph (high sodium) fills the bony labyrinth around the membranous labyrinth, which contains endolymph.

questions.stem: Endolymph differs from perilymph in being rich in
questions.why: Endolymph is high in potassium and low in sodium, resembling intracellular fluid; perilymph is the reverse.

questions.stem: Endolymph is produced chiefly by the
questions.why: The stria vascularis in the cochlear duct secretes endolymph; perilymph is formed by capillaries of the endosteum.

questions.stem: The sensory organ of hearing, the spiral organ of Corti, rests on the
questions.why: The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane within the scala media (cochlear duct).

questions.stem: The membrane separating the scala vestibuli from the scala media is
questions.why: Reissner's membrane forms the roof of the cochlear duct, separating scala media from scala vestibuli; the basilar membrane forms its floor.

questions.stem: The base of the basilar membrane (near the oval window) is narrow and stiff, so it responds best to
questions.why: The stiff narrow base detects high frequencies; the wide flexible apex detects low frequencies (tonotopy).

questions.stem: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex of the cochlea at the
questions.why: The two perilymph-filled scalae are continuous at the helicotrema at the cochlear apex.

questions.stem: The semicircular canals detect
questions.why: The three semicircular canals, via the crista ampullaris, detect angular (rotational) movements of the head.

questions.stem: The utricle and saccule detect linear acceleration and head position by means of their
questions.why: The maculae of the utricle and saccule, with their otoconia, sense linear acceleration and gravity (static equilibrium).

questions.stem: The spiral ganglion, containing the cell bodies of the cochlear nerve, lies within the
questions.why: The spiral ganglion is housed in the modiolus, the central bony core of the cochlea.

questions.stem: Otosclerosis, abnormal bone growth fixing the stapes at the oval window, typically causes
questions.why: Fixation of the stapes impairs mechanical sound conduction, giving a conductive hearing loss.

questions.stem: Age-related sensorineural hearing loss is known as
questions.why: Presbycusis is progressive sensorineural loss of high-frequency hearing with age.
